title: Concavity and the Second Derivative Test
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: The second derivative f'' describes concavity, the way a graph bends, since f'' is the derivative of the slope function f'.
Where f''(x) > 0 the graph is concave up, curving like a cup, and the slopes f' are increasing.
Where f''(x) < 0 the graph is concave down, curving like a cap, and the slopes f' are decreasing.
Concavity is independent of direction: a function can be increasing while concave down (leveling off) or increasing while concave up (steepening).
An inflection point is where concavity changes, from concave up to concave down or vice versa.
Inflection points occur where f''(x) = 0 or is undefined AND f'' actually changes sign there.
A zero of f'' does not guarantee an inflection point: f(x) = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but f''(x) = 12x² stays positive, so the concavity never changes.
To find concavity, compute f'', solve f'' = 0 and find where f'' is undefined, test the sign of f'' in each interval, and confirm sign changes for inflection points.
Example: for f(x) = x⁴ − 6x², f''(x) = 12(x − 1)(x + 1), giving inflection points at x = −1 and x = 1.
For that function, f is concave up on (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞) and concave down on (−1, 1).
The Second Derivative Test classifies a critical point with f'(c) = 0: if f''(c) < 0 it is a local maximum, if f''(c) > 0 it is a local minimum.
If f''(c) = 0 or is undefined, the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive and the First Derivative Test must be used instead.
The Second Derivative Test is fast because it requires plugging only one value into f'', not building a full sign chart for f'.
Example: for f(x) = x³ − 3x, f''(x) = 6x; at x = 1, f''(1) = 6 > 0 gives a local minimum, and at x = −1, f''(−1) = −6 < 0 gives a local maximum.
When the Second Derivative Test fails because f''(c) = 0, the First Derivative Test still works: f(x) = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but f' changes − to + at 0, a minimum.
The First Derivative Test is the reliable fallback because it has no gaps, unlike the Second Derivative Test at points where f'' = 0 or is undefined.
The second derivative measures how fast the slope is changing, which is why it equals acceleration when the function is position over time.
For a growing quantity, f'' > 0 means the growth rate is increasing (a boom) and f'' < 0 means the growth rate is decreasing (approaching saturation).
An inflection point marks the moment a trend stops accelerating and begins to decelerate, such as the peak in daily new cases of an epidemic.
The Second Derivative Test is essentially the First Derivative Test in disguise, with f''(c) indicating whether f' is increasing or decreasing through zero.
On free response, an inflection point must be justified by stating that f'' changes sign there, not merely that f'' = 0.
All four combinations of direction (sign of f') and concavity (sign of f'') occur, and together they describe every local shape of a smooth curve.
